title: Zhu Xiaohu: China's AIGC applications have already exploded, they're just all hidden in to B
dek: Zhu Xiaohu says China's AIGC applications have already exploded, it's just all happening in enterprise services: delivery-rider accident insurance payout ratio dropped from 150 yuan to 60 yuan, video interviews hit 1 million sessions a year, and consumers never see any of it.
why: For anyone who assumes China's AIGC is nothing but wrappers: a batch of to B companies that don't burn money and are already profitable get named. The first ten-odd minutes repeat the same points a lot.
who: Early-stage investors and founders building to B AI applications, especially teams agonizing over whether to train their own model.
skip: 44:00-46:30 covers personal preferences and McKinsey-style training, low information density.

points.h: The moat is data, not the model
points.body: Fancy Tech is the example he keeps bringing out: when he invested in 2022 revenue was only a bit over 10 million, last year it did over 50 million, up five or six times, and it's profitable. The barrier isn't at the model layer — anyone can tweak Llama — it's in the data: the US has no product short-video data, US e-commerce is basically still stuck on images, while China converted entirely to short video over the past three years. The second layer is the effect feedback loop: about 60% to 70% of customers authorize him to monitor ad performance, so he knows exactly which videos suit Taobao, which suit Xiaohongshu, which suit Douyin, and catching up later is not easy. The third layer is sales management capability.

points.h: Neither money nor headcount buys you PMF
points.body: Zhu Xiaohu breaks the AIGC threshold into two things: finding PMF, and managing sales. The former has nothing to do with headcount or cost — in his words, if ten people can't find it, a hundred people won't find it either, so throwing tens of millions of yuan at a large model is equally futile. His own cadence is to invest 20-30 million RMB first, then add more if it goes well. The second scarce capability is sales management: most founders building large models don't know how to manage sales and don't understand commercialization; the AI video interview company he backed raised only one-tenth of what its competitors raised, the competitors all died, and it is the only company in all of China that can do human-machine double-blind testing and the only one that can do machine follow-up questions.

In the first half of 2023, while the Four Little Dragons were still crossing the cycle, he concluded these large-model companies were hopeless and didn't talk to a single one, including Wang Huiwen, whom he knew well. The reason wasn't technology: no scenarios, no data, and valuations were that expensive from the start, a billion dollars in the first round. He judged the outcome might be worse than the Four Little Dragons: the Dragons had a golden period early on and revenue climbed fast; large models have no revenue and still have to do research. His most piercing question: if you spend big money to build a GPT-4-level model and someone open-sources it, all that money is wasted — apart from the big platforms, which startup would dare?

points.h: Antitrust has sealed off the large-model exit
points.body: Someone asked him, if you had 100 million dollars and absolutely had to invest in large models, how would you invest. He said he told Wang Xiaochuan at a conference: if there were no antitrust, he'd be willing to invest in Wang Xiaochuan — solid technology, solid person, decent relations with the big platforms, at least he could sell to Tencent or Alibaba. But with antitrust, he doesn't know how to exit, so he doesn't invest. He contrasts with Dianxin: in the early mobile internet era everyone built localized OSes, Dianxin eventually sold to Baidu and the fund made a little money, because back then there was no antitrust. Today large-model companies wanting to wait for a big-platform acquisition find that road sealed off.

points.h: Open source catching closed source is only a matter of time
points.body: His argument is on the order of engineer counts: OpenAI has only one or two hundred engineers, while open source has millions, tens of millions of engineers using it worldwide — how could you stay behind forever? Closed source leads today because OpenAI's technology iteration curve is still fairly steep, maybe a year or even a year and a half ahead; but the curve will flatten someday, and then open source catches up in one leap, just like Android caught iOS. His criterion is hard: whether 100,000 cards can still brute-force a miracle. If they can, then sure, impressive; if they can't significantly improve performance, iteration slows and open source catches up immediately. He also cites Silicon Valley: the secrets are inside OpenAI and Anthropic and a few other companies, they have no talent drain, so short-term catching up is hard.

points.h: Large-model pricing hit the floor within a year
points.body: This is his most concrete strike against large-model commercialization: in early 2023, private deployment of a large model was quoted at 10 million; by June it was 5 million; by year-end even 1 million was too much, a central SOE deployment for under 1 million RMB. In one year, the price hit the floor. He contrasts this with the Four Little Dragons: the Dragons had it much easier monetizing back then, because their solutions were significantly better than traditional ones and there was little competition — only five, six, seven, eight players in the market, with two or three golden years to build revenue first before the price war started. Large models don't even get that golden period.

points.h: The explosion has already happened, it's just all in to B
points.body: This is his most counterintuitive line: applications have already exploded, it's just all to B, so consumers have no idea. The examples are concrete: delivery-rider accident insurance — insurers used to collect 100 yuan in premiums and pay out 150, because verifying claims cost too much; now the rider makes a call and films a walkaround video of the scene, payouts drop from 150 to 60, and insurers start making money. Another: China's traditional marketing calls, a market of four to five hundred billion a year — US carriers are monopolized by FaceTime and don't support C2C video calls, China does, so an ordinary phone call turns into a virtual livestream, letting a celebrity make a video livestream call to you, conversion rate at least doubles.

points.h: Everyone who listened to us is still alive today
points.body: His one-line mantra for founders from start to finish: don't burn money. This isn't PR talk — he says he's been telling portfolio companies not to burn money since 2021, those who listened adjusted pretty well, those who wouldn't listen were the ones who raised too much money and thought they were hot stuff, and now they're starting to face reality. His way of teaching companies to budget: assume in the base case that revenue drops 2% and you can break even; never assume revenue growth, because the moment you assume growth you spend the costs first, and if revenue falls short you're in trouble. He says this is the consensus in the investment world this year: no company should burn money, treat every round as the last round.
